vignette:
Minh is a 34-year-old Vietnamese-American hospital chaplain, widowed two years ago when his wife died in a car accident. The grief had already carved a deep guilt into him—he should have been driving, should have seen the other car, should have been able to stop it. That sense of helplessness was still raw when, six months ago, he was mugged at gunpoint in the parking lot after a late shift. The assailant pressed a pistol into his ribs, breathing hard and fast, reeking of sweat and cheap cologne. Minh handed over his wallet without a word, but the experience burned into him. Now he cannot escape the images that arrive without warning: the glint of the barrel, the man's red-rimmed eyes. Sometimes the smell of that sweat comes back—a phantom odor that makes his stomach turn. And beneath the fear, a hot rage that he never anticipated. He is angry at the mugger, yes, but more at himself. "The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am," he tells his therapist, his voice flat. A chaplain should be calm, should know how to de-escalate, should not have been walking alone at that hour. Somebody else—a bigger man, a streetwise man—would not have gotten into this situation. He has come to believe that bad things simply happen to him and he cannot stop them; the car accident proved it, and now the mugging has confirmed it. That belief itself seems to call the memory forward, as if each intrusion is a reminder that he was right all along—that he is helpless and marked for misfortune.

That belief shapes how he moves through the world. Because he is certain he cannot prevent disaster, he scans every entering face for threat. The crowded hospital cafeteria becomes a danger zone; he stands with his back to the wall, watching the door, anticipating attack. His hypervigilance ensures he notices every heavy breather—a runner on the sidewalk, a patient gasping for air in the ward—and each time the sound sends his heart racing, pulling him back to the mugger's labored panting. A visitor who shares the same build as the assailant triggers a cascade of images: the gun, the eyes, the smell. He has started avoiding certain hallways and the subway entirely; the crush of commuters feels like a trap. His daily rounds have shrunk. He used to move freely through every floor as a chaplain; now he sticks to the chapel and his office, pleading paperwork when asked to visit the emergency department.

The memories themselves reinforce his appraisals. When the image of the gun intrudes, or when the phantom sweat smell catches him mid-sentence, he thinks, See—you're still stuck, you're still weak, you cannot move on. That only deepens the character blame. And the rage he feels on recall—a hot, righteous fury—frightens him profoundly. A chaplain should forgive, should be compassionate. That he can feel such rage tells him he is fundamentally flawed, which makes him more vigilant for signs of danger, more likely to interpret a crowded room as a place where he will be singled out again. After a flashback he finds himself flinching at footsteps, his eyes darting to exits, as if the mugging is about to happen again. The cycle tightens: the more he scans, the more triggers he finds; the more triggers he finds, the more memories erupt; and each memory confirms his helplessness and self-blame.

He has stopped attending the grief group he started after his wife died; he cannot bear the crowded room, the heavy sighs of mourners. Last week he snapped at a nurse who tapped him on the shoulder from behind—he spun around, heart pounding, nearly shouting. He apologized, but the nurse looked worried. What finally brought him to seek help was the moment he realized he was avoiding the hospital chapel itself—because the candles there smelled faintly of wax and something like the assailant's cologne. He had nowhere left to go. He is terrified that if he does not get better, he will lose his vocation, the only thing that has given his life meaning since his wife died. And he is afraid that facing the memories will only prove what he already believes: that he is the sort of person bad things happen to, and there is no escaping that.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not show negative appraisals directly leading to memory intrusions; they lead to hypervigilance which increases trigger detection, which then leads to memories, but no direct causal relationship from negative appraisals to memory is depicted.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not show negative appraisals directly leading to memory intrusions; they lead to hypervigilance which increases trigger detection, which then leads to memories, but no direct causal relationship from negative appraisals to memory is depicted.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
